title: Pipedream Workflows is shutting down: How to export workflows and move to Zapier
summary: Pipedream Workflows is shutting down March 31, 2027. Here's how to export your workflows, rebuild them as Zaps, and test everything before the deadline.
body_markdown:
[Pipedream Workflows is shutting down](https://pipedream.com/docs/workflows) on March 31, 2027, along with String, Pipedream's AI agent builder. Pipedream will permanently delete all Workflows data by April 30, 2027. If you have workflows running there, you'll need to export them and rebuild them somewhere else before then.


Here's how to export your Pipedream Workflows data and rebuild them as Zaps (Zapier's automated workflows) before the deadline. I'll also cover why Zapier is your best option compared to other Pipedream Workflows alternatives.


[Pipedream Connect](https://zapier.com/compare/zapier-vs-pipedream) , which lets developers add app integrations and agent tools to their own product or AI agent, isn't affected. Only Workflows and String are.

## Key dates for transferring your Pipedream Workflows data


If you have existing automations in Pipedream, they'll keep running normally until the cutoff. But keep these dates in mind:


-


**March 31, 2027:** Workflows and String will shut down. Active subscriptions will be canceled automatically, with a prorated refund.


-


**April 30, 2027:** All Workflows data will be permanently deleted, including the credentials and OAuth tokens for your connected accounts.


As you plan your migration to another automation platform, I recommend building in more of a buffer than feels necessary. Pipedream's export tool works one project at a time, and you should let a rebuilt Zap run for a few days next to the original before you retire it.


## Step 1: Export your Pipedream workflows


Pipedream has[an export tool](https://pipedream.com/docs/workflows/export-workflows) that packs a project's workflows into a .zip archive, with one JSON file per workflow. The export works as a blueprint for rebuilding. Zapier doesn't import Pipedream's format directly, but you can hand these files to your AI tool or Zapier's AI builder and have it rebuild each workflow as a Zap (more on that in Step 2).


Here's how to export a project:


1.


Open the project in your[Pipedream dashboard](https://pipedream.com/projects) , then select **Settings** in the left navigation.


2.


Click **Export Workflows** at the bottom of the settings panel. Pipedream builds the archive in the background.


3.


When the export finishes, select **File Store** in the project's left navigation and download` project_export-<project_id>.zip` .


Each project can have one export at a time, so if you change a workflow and want a fresh export, delete the old .zip first. Also, one export covers up to 500 workflows or 256 MB of workflow content, whichever comes first, so a big project may need to be split up and exported in pieces.


### What's in the export


Each workflow's JSON file holds the latest deployed version of the workflow: its triggers, its steps in order, the values you configured on each step, and the steps inside any if/else or switch branches. The archive also includes a` manifest.json` that lists every workflow in the project, flags any that were skipped, and names each step and prop you'll need to re-enter or reconnect later.


Here's what the export leaves out, which means you'll need to handle them on your own:


-


Secret values and environment variables


-


Connected accounts (credentials and OAuth tokens are never exported)


-


Event history, data stores, and File Store files


-


Code for private multi-file components, which only appear as a component key


### Save a few real examples before you rebuild


Event history doesn't come with the export, so you'll have nothing to compare your new Zap against unless you grab it now. For the workflows that matter most, copy a handful of real inputs and the outputs they produced from Pipedream. Once your Zap is built, run the same inputs through it and check that the results match.


## Step 2: Rebuild your workflows as Zaps


Rebuilding your workflows means reconnecting your apps and testing each Zap before you retire the original. You don't have to recreate every trigger and action by hand, though: your AI tool or Zapier's AI builder can draft the Zap from your export. Since Zapier supports[10,000+ apps](https://zapier.com/apps) , most of your connections will carry over directly.


You have a few ways to do the building itself. No matter which way you build, start by[signing up for Zapier](https://zapier.com/sign-up) (it's free).


### 1. Have your AI tool build the workflow


You can[add Zapier to any AI agent](https://zapier.com/blog/zapier-mcp-guide/) , including ChatGPT, Claude, or Cursor. Find it in the agent's connector library, or ask your agent to "connect to Zapier." Describe what the workflow does, attach or paste the export from Pipedream, and the AI tool builds a Zap that keeps running on Zapier after the chat is over. Zapier handles each app's login, so you'll never paste an API key into the conversation.


Here's a prompt you can use:


Prompt


```text
Use Zapier to rebuild this Pipedream workflow as a Zap. Keep the same trigger, steps, and branching. Use built-in Zapier steps wherever you can, and Code by Zapier only for steps that run custom code. Tell me which apps I need to reconnect. The workflow's exported JSON is below.
```


Only open the Zap in the visual editor if you want to check it, since your AI tool can make changes too. Zapier shows what the Zap does and anything it still needs from you, such as connecting an app.


### 2. Or describe it to Zapier's AI builder


You can also start inside Zapier. Zapier's AI builder drafts a Zap from a description of what you want. If you don't have a Zapier account yet, create one, then start a new Zap from your[Zapier dashboard](https://zapier.com/app/home) .


Paste in the workflow's exported JSON (or a plain-language summary of what the workflow does) with a line at the top telling the builder what to do with it.


You can use that same prompt here:


Prompt


```text
Rebuild this Pipedream workflow as a Zap. Keep the same trigger, steps, and branching. Use built-in Zapier steps wherever you can, and Code by Zapier only for steps that run custom code. The workflow's exported JSON is below.
```


### 3. For code-heavy workflows, build it in code


If a workflow is mostly custom code, you don't have to break it into app steps. You can[write and run TypeScript in the Zap's code editor](https://help.zapier.com/hc/en-us/articles/49005047515021-Use-the-Workflow-Manager-to-build-and-view-your-Next-Gen-Zaps) , alongside the AI assistant and visual canvas, which makes Pipedream's Node.js steps the easiest to carry over.


For a single step that needs custom logic inside a Zap,[Code by Zapier](https://help.zapier.com/hc/en-us/articles/45405528551181-Using-Code-by-Zapier) runs JavaScript or Python, and on paid plans you can import public npm and PyPI packages. Go and Bash steps need to be rewritten in one of those languages either way.


## Step 3. Review, reconnect your apps, and test


However the Zap gets built, you'll still need to connect each app. Pipedream's export strips out credentials (that's a good thing), so every app needs to be authenticated again on the Zapier side.


You'll get prompts from Zapier (or the AI tool you're building in) to authenticate your app connections. Once you've connected all your apps, Zapier will run a test with sample data. It's a good idea to compare the results with the real examples you saved from Pipedream.


Keep chatting to tweak the Zap until you're happy with the output, then publish the workflow.


One thing to keep in mind: if the Pipedream workflow and the new Zap both fire on the same event, they'll both do their jobs. That means your Slack channel or spreadsheet will get everything twice. Point the new Zap at a test destination while you check it, then turn off the Pipedream workflow once your Zap is published.


## Pipedream alternatives and why Zapier fits


I might be a die-hard Zapier fan (and have been since before I worked here), but Zapier isn't the only place you can land after leaving Pipedream Workflows.[n8n](https://zapier.com/compare/zapier-vs-n8n/) and[Make](https://zapier.com/compare/zapier-vs-make/) are popular options, and either can handle your existing workflows. For a full rundown, see our list of the[best Pipedream alternatives](https://zapier.com/blog/pipedream-alternatives/) . But I'd argue neither of them will make the move as painless as Zapier will.


n8n is built for engineering-led teams that want full control over their own infrastructure. It connects to roughly 1,500 apps, and much of its flexibility comes from writing JavaScript expressions and code nodes, which will feel familiar if you're used to Pipedream's code steps. The tradeoff is who owns the operational risk.


Zapier handles retries, error handling, and security patches automatically, and it processes 3 billion workflow runs a month without you thinking about any of it. On n8n, all of that unglamorous work, plus the hosting bill if you self-host, is on you.


Make is the more visual option. It's a node-based builder that connects to about 3,500 apps, and its Routers, Iterators, and Aggregators give you powerful branching logic. That power comes at a cost, though. Make's own team recommends around 19 hours of coursework before you build anything complex, which is a lot to ask when you're rebuilding a stack of workflows against a deadline.


Zapier is the more direct move for what Pipedream users need. It connects to 10,000+


apps, and you can hand an exported workflow to your AI tool or Zapier's AI builder and get a first draft of the Zap instead of starting from a blank canvas. When a step needs custom logic, you can write TypeScript in the Zap's code editor or run JavaScript or Python with Code by Zapier. And the governance you'll eventually need, like granular permissions and approval workflows, is already built for teams at very different scales—including 69% of the Fortune 1000.


But since you're on the Zapier blog, don't take my word for it. At[ClickUp](https://zapier.com/customer-stories/clickup) , Senior Technical Support Engineer Corey Smith built an MCP-powered Zendesk triage system that cut research from 15 minutes to 4 minutes per ticket across about 5,000 tickets a month, saving the support team 917+ hours monthly. And[Vetano](https://zapier.com/blog/vetano-next-gen-zaps/) 's founder, Chris Fairley, could have had Claude write his hand-offs as code but chose Zapier instead. As he put it, "You can go inside of Zapier, you can see your history, what Zaps went. It's just the whole graphical side of it. It would take tons to try to replicate." Both are proof that technical teams can run serious workflows on Zapier and still see exactly what's happening inside them.

## Pipedream migration FAQ


### When does Pipedream Workflows shut down?


Pipedream Workflows and String shut down on March 31, 2027. Pipedream will permanently delete all Workflows data by April 30, 2027. Your workflows keep running normally until March 31.


### Can I import my Pipedream export into Zapier?


Kind of. The export is a .zip file with one JSON file per workflow, which works as a reference for rebuilding. The quickest way to rebuild is to give the workflow's JSON or a plain-language summary to your AI tool or Zapier's AI builder and review what it creates.


### Can I move code-heavy workflows to Zapier?


Yes. Zaps can be built in code as well as in the editor or by an AI tool, and you can write and run TypeScript in the Zap's code editor. Code by Zapier also runs JavaScript or Python for a single step. Go and Bash steps need to be rewritten in one of those languages.


### What happens to my connected accounts and credentials?


They aren't included in the export, and Pipedream deletes those credentials along with the rest of your Workflows data by April 30, 2027. You'll need to reconnect each app in Zapier when you rebuild, and re-enter any secrets or environment variables.


### Does the shutdown affect Pipedream Connect?


No. Connect, including its API, MCP servers, and proxy, shouldn't be affected. This guide is for people moving off Workflows.


### What happens to my Pipedream subscription?


Subscriptions stay active until March 31, 2027, then Pipedream will cancel them automatically with a prorated refund. Monthly subscribers can cancel sooner from their account settings, and annual subscribers can contact Pipedream support for an early cancellation and prorated refund.


### How many workflows can I export at once?


One export covers a single project, up to 500 workflows or 256 MB of workflow content. If a project goes over either limit,` manifest.json` marks the remaining workflows as skipped. Move those skipped workflows into another project and then export that one, too.
